title: The Difference Between Being Calm and Being Numb
author: Dr Stoic Wisdom
summary: The writer opens with a confession that for two years he practiced Stoicism as emotional suppression, flattening his face at insults and swallowing frustration at work while calling it resilience. He names that a slow disconnection from his own life dressed up as philosophy. The argument matters, he claims, because the culture has correctly learned that suppressing emotion damages people, and because Stoic has become internet shorthand for unbothered, the critique is landing on a tradition built to warn against exactly that. His central distinction is between numbness, which is refusing to feel something, and equanimity, which is feeling it completely and then deciding with a clear head what to do. The illustrative case is Seneca writing to Marcia three years into grief for her son: not a command to stop grieving, but a warning that unexamined grief stops being a room you pass through and becomes a place you live. He offers a usable diagnostic. After something that should have affected you, ask whether you metabolized it or simply did not let it in, and treat the ability to describe what you felt, when it peaked, and how it shifted as the marker of the real practice. He argues most people who pick up Stoicism as self-help burn out within a year because a lid eventually fails, and that the tradition aimed at people who could feel the full weight of something hard and still act well.
points: The wall and floor image carries the argument: a wall keeps weather out, while a good floor lets you stand while the weather moves through you.
Seneca's letter to Marcia is read as an instruction to notice what you do with a feeling after it arrives, not to stop having it.
The self-test is diagnostic rather than moral, distinguishing a describable arc of feeling from a gray flatness where the feeling should have been.
He attributes the high burnout rate among self-help Stoics to using the philosophy as a lid, and reframes the practice as translation from feeling into judgment about control and wise action.
Marcus Aurelius writing privately at night about frustration, envy, and exhaustion is offered as evidence the Stoics named emotions plainly rather than performing tranquility.
quotes: I thought the goal was to feel less. Someone would say something cutting, and I’d flatten my face and think, a Stoic wouldn’t react. Something would go wrong at work, and I’d swallow the frustration whole and call it resilience. I got quieter. Harder to read. I mistook this for progress.

Numbness is what happens when you refuse to feel something. Equanimity is what happens when you feel it completely, and then decide, with a clear head, what to do about it. A wall keeps weather out. A good floor just lets you stand while the weather moves through.

He told her that grief left unexamined stops being a room you pass through and becomes a place you live. His argument wasn’t feel nothing. It was closer to: notice what you’re doing with the feeling once it arrives.
You can’t skip the feeling and land on the wisdom anyway. The feeling is what the wisdom is made out of.
Most people who pick up Stoicism as a self-help tool burn out on it within a year, and I think this is why. They’re using it as a lid. A lid fails eventually.

Next time you notice that flat, unbothered feeling after something that should have affected you, a real loss, a real insult, a real disappointment, ask yourself one question. Did I metabolize this, or did I just not let it in.

The Stoics weren’t trying to build people who felt less. They were trying to build people who could feel the full weight of something hard and still act well, which is a much harder and much more human thing to pull off than simply not feeling.
Not less feeling. Just a better relationship with the feeling you already have. The goal was never to become a wall.
